activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
story:
Brielle sat at Grandma's kitchen table with a blank page in front of her and a problem the size of the whole page. On Monday, Miss Ortega had assigned a five-paragraph persuasive essay with a real introduction and a real conclusion, and it was mandatory for everyone in the class. Brielle had to persuade her readers of something, and she had chosen the hardest thing she could think of: her mother should let her adopt the stray cat that had been thriving in the alley behind the school since October.

"You've been staring at that paper for a long time," Grandpa said, setting down two mugs of cocoa.

"I know what I want to say. I just don't know how to make anybody believe it." She slid her notes across the table. On them she had scribbled three words she'd copied off a library book when she was hunting for essay tips: ethos, pathos, logos.

Grandpa squinted at the words, then smiled in a way that made his whole face crinkle. "Ethos, pathos, logos. My old philosophy professor would be proud. In his Rhetoric, Aristotle described three ways to persuade: ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, logic and evidence."

Brielle wrote fast, then stopped. "Wait. That means there's more than one door into somebody's head." She looked at her notes again. Her first attempt had been all pathos, she realized. The cat is cold. The cat is lonely. The cat has sad eyes. Her mother would just say, "There are sad cats everywhere, Brielle," and close the door. But what if she arranged the doors differently?

She decided to test it. For her introduction she would use ethos: she would explain that she had researched cat care for three weeks, that she knew the cost of food and litter, that she had already talked to the vet on Elm Street. Then logos, with evidence: the vet said a spayed cat could live fifteen years indoors, and the shelter fee was only thirty dollars, which she had saved from raking leaves. Only in the fourth paragraph would she let the cat's sad eyes appear, one paragraph of pathos, placed like the last stair at the top of a staircase.

She wrote the whole draft that afternoon, five paragraphs, and read it aloud in the living room while Grandpa listened with his hands folded. When she finished, he didn't say anything for a moment, and her heart dropped. Then he said, "If I were your mother, I'd already be looking for a litter box."

"Really?"

"You made me believe you first, then feel, then agree. That's a hard thing to do at any age." He stood and went to the hall closet and came back with a thick old book, its cover soft and worn at the corners. "This was my professor's copy. He'd want a descendant of mine to keep it."

Brielle held the book in both hands. It was heavier than it looked. "Can I read just the part with the three words?"

"Page two hundred and thirty-five," Grandpa said, tapping the spine. "Start there. Aristotle was a better teacher than I'll ever be."

She opened the book and began to read.

activity: to write a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion
story:
Dominic sat at the kitchen table with three blank pages in front of him and a pencil he had already sharpened twice. The assignment was due Monday: a five-paragraph persuasive essay, with an introduction, three reasons, and a conclusion. He had chosen the most important topic in the world, convincing his mother that he should be allowed to walk to school by himself. He wrote the first reason fast, because it was obvious. Reason one: everyone in fifth grade walks to school alone. Even the kids from the affluent streets up the hill, whose parents had every gadget money could buy, let them go. He filled two pages and then leaned back, satisfied, while his little sister Mira nibbled toast across the table.

Mira pulled the pages toward her and began to narrate his essay out loud in a dramatic voice, the way she narrated cartoons. "Everyone walks alone, so I should too." She stopped and squinted at him. "That's your big reason? Everyone?"

"So what?" Dominic said. "It's true."

"You always say Ethan's wrong about stuff even when everyone agrees with him," Mira said. "Remember when everyone said Billy took the class snacks, and you figured out it was the substitute teacher?" She slid the pages back. "Lots of people doing something doesn't make it right. That's called the bandwagon fallacy." She went back to her toast like she hadn't just knocked over his whole essay.

Dominic stared at the pages. He wanted to tell her she was wrong, but his brain kept snagging on the snack mystery. Being popular hadn't made the accusation true. So maybe being popular didn't make his reason true either. He decided to test it, the way he tested everything, on an easier target first. He wrote a new one-paragraph essay arguing that Mira should let him have the last cookie because everyone in the house wanted him to have it. He read it to her. She laughed and ate the cookie herself in one enormous bite.

"See?" she said, crumbs flying. "Nobody cares what everyone wants."

Dominic spread his three pages back out and crossed out his first reason with a long dark line. Then he wrote a new one: he knew the route, there were two crossing guards, and his friend Devi walked the same way, so they could go together. He worked until the pencil was a stub, and when his mother came home, he read the whole essay to her, introduction to conclusion, standing straight like a lawyer in a show.

She read it twice herself, silent, tapping the counter with one finger. "This is actually a real argument," she said slowly. "Saturday, we'll walk it together. If you don't forget one single safety rule, Monday you walk with Devi."

Dominic pumped his fist. Behind him, Mira whispered, "You owe me a cookie."

activity: to explain how a citizen can petition a councillor to change a local bylaw
story:
Penelope spread her homework sheet across the kitchen table, next to a plate of toast crumbs shaped, if you squinted, like a hockey rink. "Assignment," she announced to her brother Max, who was rolling a tennis ball against the thermostat on the wall. "I have to explain how a regular citizen petitions a councillor to change a bylaw. And I want to actually do it, not just write about it."

"Petition to change the bylaw that says we can't put the hockey net on the street," Max said instantly, abandoning the thermostat mid-bounce. "I've wanted that my whole life." His whole life, Penelope noted, included eleven years, four of them spent pining over that net. She pulled the city website onto her laptop, found a page listing the councillors, and picked the one whose photo had the friendliest smile. She drafted an email, added three reasons why street hockey should be legal with supervision, and hit send before Max could drip jam on the keyboard.

Two days later the reply landed. "Thank you for your message, but I'm afraid I don't represent your area," the friendly-smiling councillor wrote. "You'd need to contact the councillor for your ward." Penelope frowned at the screen. "Ward?" Max said, licking jam off his thumb. "Like a hospital?" "No, it's what the areas of the city are called," Penelope said. "I think each councillor is elected to represent one area." She tested the idea like poking a loose tooth: she typed their address into the city's ward finder, and sure enough, a map bloomed on screen, their street sitting inside a green blob labeled Ward 5. Councillor Okafor, whose photo showed a woman holding a cat, apparently belonged to them.

So Penelope conquered her embarrassment, wrote to Councillor Okafor, and mentioned that the reply had come from a councillor across town whose cat looked distinctly unimpressed. Max insisted on adding a paragraph about proportional punishment, claiming that confiscating a hockey net for a street violation was like jail for jaywalking. Penelope edited it down to one sentence. The house smelled like burnt toast again because Max had been celebrating potential victory with celebratory bread.

On Saturday, an actual letter arrived, paper and everything. "Please come to the community meeting on the twelfth," it read, "and bring your neighbours. Ten signatures will get your proposal on the agenda." Max ran upstairs yelling for their mom. Penelope counted on her fingers: the Hendersons, the Nguyens, the twins who lived in the blue house, and, if she promised to shovel their walk, old Mr. Petrakis, who yelled at the net every single winter.

"Nine," she said. "We need one more."

Max grinned and raised his hand. "I'm a citizen too, you know. I checked."

activity: to explain supply and demand using the price of strawberries in summer and winter
story:
The automatic doors of First National Bank hummed shut behind Ethan, and the smell of floor wax and cold air hit him at once. He clutched a sealed envelope with the stand's earnings and the deposit slip his mother had signed. Behind him, through the glass, his best friend Rosa guarded two nearly full jugs of strawberry lemonade and a hand-lettered sign that read "Cups $3.00." The bank closed at noon, and the clock above the teller counter read 11:41.

Ethan had set the price himself. Last summer, when strawberries were everywhere, their lemonade sold out at one dollar a cup, and there was never a drop left. He remembered standing in Rosa's grandmother's backyard in August, juice running down his wrist, watching the rows of strawberry baskets at the farm stand sell for two dollars a basket because there were so many. But that was then. In February, a single basket had cost six dollars, and Rosa had said, "See? Everybody wants them and there aren't any, so the price goes up." Ethan had turned that over all winter. More people buying than selling pushed prices one way; more selling than buying pushed them the other way. So this morning he had reasoned that three dollars a cup, fancy strawberry lemonade on a hot day, would make them rich.

It had not. At noon they had sold nine cups and poured the rest into jugs. Rosa's grandmother, waiting in the parking lot, had looked at the jugs and then at the sign. "You held your price too high," she said simply. "At three dollars, you offered cups all day long, but buyers didn't want that many at that price. Now look what's left." Ethan had stared at the jugs. It wasn't that people hated lemonade, or that the day was cold, or that the two things merely coincided to ruin their sale. It was something underneath, invisible, like the lichen spreading gray-green across the north side of the bank's stone wall, slow and steady where no one watched. The price itself had made the extra pile up.

"Next," called the teller, and Ethan stepped forward on sneakers that squeaked against the tile. He slid the envelope under the glass. The teller counted the bills, and the machine made its dry clicking sound as it stacked them.

"Deposit for the lemonade stand?" she asked.

"Yes, ma'am. Nine dollars." Ethan glanced back through the glass at Rosa, who was tapping the jug with one finger and had begun crossing out the 3 on the sign, drawing a big number 1 over it. "Tomorrow we sell it cheap," Ethan said. "We're not carrying those jugs home again."

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
story:
Dominic had fasted before, but only until lunch. This year, at Grandma Ruth's apartment, he was determined to make it all the way to sundown like the grown-ups, and he announced this at breakfast the night before while everyone was still eating. His cousin Talia, who was twelve and had diabetes, gave him a look over her glass of juice but said nothing.

The next morning the apartment smelled like nothing cooking, which felt strange. Talia sat at the table with a piece of toast, and Dominic stared at it. "You're not even trying?" he asked, feeling his stomach growl like an accusation. Last summer he had quit halfway through the day and told everyone he had a headache, and the memory still humiliated him. He wasn't going to be that kid again.

"I have to eat," Talia said. "Rabbi Felsen told my mom that when fasting would be dangerous for someone's health, Jewish law waives it. In that case, eating isn't allowed to be skipped. It's actually required." She took a bite. "So I'm doing the religious thing right now, with my toast."

Dominic tested this idea the way he tested everything, like turning a lens to see if the light would focus. If skipping the fast could be the commandment, then the day wasn't really about being hungry. He thought about his headache excuse from last summer and how he'd decided, in secret, to feel sick. He didn't say any of that out loud.

At noon, Talia checked her numbers and wrote a note on the pad by the fridge, the way she did so Grandma Ruth could see she was taking care of herself. Dominic picked up the pen and added a line below hers: "I'm still going for sundown. But if I get sick for real, I'll eat. Deal?" Talia read it, slid the pad back, and drew a small check mark with an arrow pointing at his words. Then she poured him a glass of water, set it beside his elbow, and walked away.

activity: to shade a sphere with a light source to show highlight, shadow and cast shadow
story:
Florence wanted her pencil drawing of an orange to look round instead of flat, because Grandma had promised to hang one of her drawings in the front hall if it was good enough. Grandma had a chronic habit of saying "good enough" about almost anything Florence made, but the front hall was where guests actually looked, and Florence wanted the orange to earn its spot for real.

She set a tennis ball on the kitchen table and propped her sketchbook beside it. Her first try looked like a flat circle with a gray smudge, so she clicked on the old desk lamp and dragged it close to the table. The ball lit up with a bright highlight on one side, a soft shadow underneath, and a long dark shape stretched across the table behind it. She had never noticed that before. When she raised the lamp high over the ball, the cast shadow shrank to a small puddle at its base. When she lowered it again, the shadow stretched out long and thin, like it was trying to escape across the tabletop.

"Grandma, come look at this," Florence called. Grandma came in from the garden, wiping dirt off her hands. "Watch the shadow. Low lamp, long shadow. High lamp, short shadow." She moved the lamp up and down like a slow elevator, and the shadow grew and shrank each time.

Grandna laughed. "Your grandfather used to do that with his reading lamp and his coffee mug. He'd besiege me with shadow monsters at breakfast."

Florence sharpened her pencil and started the orange again. She imagined a lamp sitting low, just past the edge of the table, and drew the cast shadow stretching far to the right, long enough to nearly touch the bowl she had added behind it. She left a small pale spot for the highlight where the imagined lamp would emit its brightest light, and she pressed harder and harder with the pencil as the shadow curled under the orange's belly.

Grandma leaned over her shoulder, still holding the gardening rag. "That one goes in the hall," she said. "Right where the light from the front window hits the wall."

story:
Rain hammered the windows of Room 12 like a monsoon that had lost its way from somewhere tropical, and inside, the chess club had dwindled to four players. Rose had spent two weeks trying to recruit new members with posters featuring a knight in sunglasses, which had attracted exactly one sixth grader named Priya, who mostly came for the snacks.

Rose was beating Marcus in six moves when he reached out, picked up his knight, studied the board, and set the knight back down on its original square without moving it. Then he reached for his rook instead.

"No," Rose said. "You touched it. You have to move it."

"That's not a rule. That's a rule you invented to win." Marcus crossed his arms. Priya stopped chewing her crackers to watch.

Rose was sure she was right, though she could not have said where she'd learned it, which bothered her the way a loose tooth bothers a tongue. She got the club's dog-eared rulebook from the shelf and flipped through it while Marcus drummed his fingers. There it was, in a paragraph about formal chess: if you deliberately touch one of your own pieces, you must move that piece, if it has a legal move.

"Touch-move," Rose read aloud. "It's called touch-move."

Marcus looked at the page for a long moment, then at his knight, which had exactly one legal move, straight into the path of her bishop. He sighed like a man carrying groceries up three flights of stairs and pushed the knight forward. "Fine. But now I know it too, and next week it's your hands I'm watching."

"Deal," Rose said, and captured the knight.

story:
Hunter wanted the last open swing before the bell, and so did Marcus. They stood toe to toe in the wood chips, neither one moving.

"Rock-paper-scissors," said Marcus. "But I always throw rock. Rock wins."

"That's not how it works," Hunter said. "Watch. Rock beats scissors, but scissors beats paper, and paper beats rock. Every choice beats one thing and loses to one thing. So rock can't be the best one, because there's no best one."

Marcus squinted at him. "Says who?"

"Let's try it. You throw rock every time. I'll figure out the pattern." Hunter could perceive the plan forming before Marcus even raised his fist, because a boy who announces rock always throws rock. They played three rounds. Rock. Paper. Marcus lost. Rock. Paper. Lost again. On the third round Marcus switched to scissors at the last second, and Hunter's paper won anyway.

"Okay," Marcus said slowly. "Okay, but that's because you're some kind of mind reader."

"It's because you told me your move. Your testimony, bro. You testified against yourself."

Marcus laughed despite himself, but then his shoulders sagged. "So what do we do? We both want the swing and we can't both have it."

Hunter picked up a stick and scratched two lines in the wood chips. "Here's the problem, named: one swing, two kids, four minutes till the bell. Now we make a rule that fits it. Two minutes each. Loser of one fair round goes second, but the winner has to swap when I count to a hundred and twenty."

"Fair round means I can throw anything?"

"Anything. Rock is versatile if nobody knows it's coming."

They shook fists. Marcus threw paper, Hunter threw rock, and Marcus whooped so loud a first grader looked over from the slide.

"Count fast," Marcus said, already pumping his legs toward the sky.

activity: to give a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points and a closing
story:
Anthony's speech was a cargo ship, and he was its captain. That was the game he had invented on the bus to the tournament: the two minutes were the harbor, his three points were cargo holds stuffed with treasure, and the judges were dockworkers who had to unload everything before the tide went out. In practice his grandfather had listened from the kitchen table, nodding along, and then halfway through he had squinted and asked, "Wait, which point is this now? Am I still on the first one?" Anthony had frozen. He knew the speech was good. He could see every argument on the page in his head, perfectly arranged. His grandfather could not. It hit Anthony like a cold splash: a listener cannot flip back a page the way a reader can. Whatever his grandfather heard was all there was. If Anthony lost him, there was no going back for the missing cargo.

In the hallway outside the debate room, Anthony tested a small idea on his teammate Priya. He delivered his opening hook, then said, "First, the plan costs too much. Second, nobody wants it. Finally, it breaks the rules." Then he asked her to close her eyes and narrate it back to him, hold by hold. She got all three, in order. He tried again without the first, second and finally, mixing them in plain sentences, and she stumbled, unsure whether the cost point came before or after the rules point. Anthony grinned. The words were working like lights on a dark channel, marking each hold so the dockworkers always knew where they were.

Room 4 was sparse, just two long tables, a clock, and a judge with a clipboard. Anthony stood, took a breath, and imagined the ship sliding into harbor. "First," he said, and watched the judge's pencil drop to the page. "Second," and it dropped again. When he finished his closing and sat down, the judge had three neat lines on the paper, one for each hold, all unloaded.

His grandfather was waiting by the water fountain. "I didn't get lost once," he said, tapping his temple. "First, second, finally. I knew where I was the whole time." Anthony said, "Hold three is still full, Grandpa. Come on, I'll unload it for you in the car."

story:
Paisley stared at the recipe card on Nova's kitchen counter like it was a treasure map with the X smudged out. "Step one says preheat the oven to three seventy-five," she read. "We have to be walking to the bus stop by noon, or we miss the bake sale." Nova's little brother, Bram, who considered himself the first tenant of every room he entered because he never left it, leaned over their shoulders to supervise.

They measured and mixed, arguing only once about whether an egg with a wobbly shell still counted as an egg. "It contributes the same amount of egg," Nova said, cracking it with a flourish. Paisley folded in the blueberries, dropped the batter into twelve cups, and slid the tin into the oven just as the clock said eleven twenty. Then she sat on the floor and watched the oven light like it was television.

At eleven fifty the timer beeped. Paisley pulled the tin out, and both girls frowned. The muffin tops looked pale, not golden like the picture on the card. "They can't be done," Nova said. "But the timer said." Paisley gazed at the pale tops and considered the issue. The outsides were clues, but the real answer was hidden inside, where no one could see. She grabbed a toothpick, pushed it into the centre of the tallest muffin, and pulled it out. Wet batter clung to the wood. "Not done," she announced, feeling like a detective. She set the timer again and put the tin back in.

The second time, the tops had browned, and when she pushed a toothpick into the centre of another muffin, it came out clean except for a few dry crumbs. "Done!" Nova cheered. They wrapped the muffins in a dish towel and sprinted for the bus, arriving with one minute to spare. At the bake sale, the muffins sold out in twenty minutes, leaving behind only an impoverished plate of crumbs. Bram looked at it and said, "I'll take those."

activity: to sing in two-part harmony with a choir and hold their part against the other
story:
Noah had been dreading Thursday choir practice ever since the music room got picked for renovation, because now forty kids crammed into the cafeteria, which smelled like Tuesday's mystery cuisine and echoed like a gym. Mr. Reyes wanted the two groups to sing "Row, Row, Row Your Boat" as a round, and Noah's group kept crashing into the other group's line.

"It's not a contest," Mr. Reyes called out. "Group One, you begin. Group Two, you wait for my cue."

Group One started. Noah counted quietly, waiting, but when his group came in, his ears played a trick on him. The first group's voices slid into his head and dragged his pitch along, so that by "gently down the stream" he was singing their notes, not his. Half his group did the same thing. The round collapsed into a pile of noise, and Priya from Group One laughed so hard she snorted.

Noah stared at the piano. Something was strange, he thought. Both groups were singing exactly the same melody, the same words, the same tune. Nobody was singing anything different. So where was the harmony coming from? It had to be the starting times. Group One began, and Group Two came in later, and that was the only difference anywhere. Same song, different moments. He wondered if that alone could be what made the two parts fit.

"Can we try it slower?" he asked. "I want to test something."

Mr. Reyes raised an eyebrow but agreed. This time Noah didn't listen to Group One at all. He watched Mr. Reyes's hand, kept his own melody going like a train on its own track, and let the other voices wash past him. When he dared to listen again, his line and Group One's line were leaning against each other, and the sound was suddenly wide, like two colors side by side.

"It's the same melody," Noah said afterward, grabbing his backpack. "We're both singing the same thing. We just start at different times, and that's what makes the harmony."

"That's a round," Priya said. "It's called a round."

"I like it," Noah said. "Which part do you like better, ours or yours?"

"That's subjective," Priya said, and Noah laughed and held the door for her.

story:
The rain had stopped by lunch, so the whole grade migrated to the four-square court behind the gym, where the pavement was already dry under the big oak. Jaxon got a square right away, which almost never happened. By the third round it was him and a boy named Derek from Mrs. Alvarez's class, and Derek was good, fast with his hands and patient, waiting for a mistake.

The score was close when Jaxon's bounce clipped the corner line. Derek called it out, Jaxon said it was in, and for a moment the game just stopped. Then Derek said, "New rule. Line balls are in from now on." Jaxon noticed that Derek's next serve would land exactly where that corner was, and that the "new rule" would hand him the game. The other two players shifted their weight and looked at the ground.

Jaxon picked up the ball instead of serving it. "The problem isn't whether that ball was in or out," he said. "The problem is that we never decided what a line ball counts as. So nobody's wrong and everybody's mad." Derek frowned, but he didn't argue, because it was true. Jaxon went on, feeling his way through it. "If you make a rule right when it wins you the game, it isn't really a rule. It's just you grabbing the point. Agreeing on a rule before we start is fairer, because nobody knows yet whether it'll help them or hurt them. You can't cheat with a rule you agreed to when it could still go either way."

Nobody said anything for a second. Then the girl in the second square, Priya, said, "So we call the game, agree on the line rule out loud, and replay from the start of this rally." Jaxon nodded. "Exactly. Make it explicit now, while it's still even." Derek turned the word over, then shrugged. "Line balls are in," he said clearly, so everyone heard it. "Say it back so we all own it." Three voices said it back.

They replayed the rally, and this time Derek's serve did clip the line, and the line was in, and Jaxon lost the point and then the square. He walked to the end of the line, dusting chalk off his palms, and Priya followed him with the rubber ball under her arm.

"That was a good game," she said. Jaxon watched Derek hit a clean shot into the far corner, no line involved at all. "Next time we start," he said, "I'm writing the rules on the wall first." Priya grinned and tossed him the ball. "Better use pencil. Chalk washes off in the rain."

story:
The deodorant aisle at Rite Aid had forty-two options, and Isla had exactly seven minutes before her dad finished at the prescription counter. She picked up a blue stick, sniffed it, and put it back. Her armpits had turned on her three weeks ago, right after track practice, and no amount of wishing had switched them off again.

Today at lunch, Marta had slid her tray half a foot down the table. Isla had pretended not to notice, but she noticed. She had also skipped her shower last night, because she was tired, and again this morning, because she was late. That was the pattern, she realized, standing there between the powder-fresh and the unscented. Practice, then no shower, then Marta's tray sliding away. On the days she showered right after practice, nobody moved.

"Interesting," she whispered, and a woman sorting shelves nearby gave her a look.

Her dad was already deep in a controversy with the pharmacist about whether the generic medicine was the same as the brand name. Isla left them to it. She tested her idea right there, lifting one arm in the aisle like she was reaching for the top shelf. The smell rose, unmistakable. Then she thought about the girl who showered every day and still used deodorant, and how that girl had never cleared a room in her life. So deodorant alone wasn't the whole answer. Something invisible was going on, something you couldn't see, only smell.

"There you are," her dad said, dropping the bag in the cart. "You vanished."

"I'm solving a case." She held up the blue stick. "Can we get this?"

He looked at her, then at the stick, and something passed across his face. "You know, your mom's been leaving the bathroom door open as a hint."

"I figured it out myself," Isla said. "Tonight, soap first, then this. Every day. I'll comply."

"That's my detective," he said, and steered the cart toward the registers.

At school the next morning, Marta slid her tray closer instead.

activity: to build a simple circuit with a battery, a switch and a bulb and explain why it lights
story:
Elena spread her circuit kit on the flat bottom of the halfpipe, where the concrete was still shaded at nine in the morning. By noon the skaters would migrate to the cool side of the park, but for now she had the whole bowl to herself. Her science project was due Monday: build a circuit with a battery, a switch, and a bulb, then explain why the bulb lit. The building part she could do. The explaining part was the problem.

She clipped a wire to the battery's positive terminal, ran it to the switch, ran another wire from the switch to the bulb, and connected a final wire back to the negative terminal. She snapped the switch shut. The bulb glowed. So far so good. Then she opened her textbook to copy the diagram, and the arrows stopped her cold. They pointed from positive to negative, but in the margin of the library copy, someone had written in pencil, "The electrons in the wires actually move the other way, negative to positive. The arrows lie."

Elena read the note three times. She flipped the battery in its holder so the terminals were reversed, and the bulb still lit. story:
Kaylee spread her supplies across the kitchen table: a box of mixed beads, a styrofoam ball, thin floral wire, and a crumpled assignment sheet. Due tomorrow. Build a model of a carbon atom with every particle in its right place. She had put it off for three days, and now her little brother Dex was circling the table like a shark, snacking on the pretzels she had set aside as motivation.

"Red for protons," she muttered, sorting beads into piles. "Blue for neutrons." She lifted a bead, considering. Her class notes said protons have a positive charge, electrons have a negative charge, and neutrons have no charge at all. That last part had snagged in her brain all afternoon. Positive and negative made sense, like the ends of the magnets on the fridge, but a particle that just sat there doing nothing charge-wise seemed like a flaw in the design. "Ironic," she said out loud, "that the boring ones are what make the atom heavy."

"What's ironic?" Dex asked, stealing a pretzel.

"Nothing. Wait, actually." She held up a yellow bead. "Electrons have to be yellow. They're the fast ones, the flashy ones. And protons are red because they're positive, like a plus sign. Electrons are negative." She frowned at the blue pile. "Neutrons are the ones with no charge at all. So they can't be red or yellow. They need their own color so nobody gets confused."

"White," said Dex, with his mouth full.

Kaylee stared at him. White. Neutral, blank, nothing written on it. She tested the idea by labeling a scrap of paper: red equals positive, yellow equals negative, white equals no charge. A stranger picking up the model could read it like a map. "Dex, you might be an artisan and not even know it."

"What's an artisan?"

"Somebody who makes things really well. Now stop eating my supplies." She cut six lengths of wire and started pushing beads into the big foam ball, six red and six white packed together in the middle for the nucleus. Her first attempt was lopsided, so she pulled the beads out and tried again, spacing them evenly so the ball wouldn't wobble when she hung it. For the electrons she bent wire loops around the sphere, two in the inner ring and four in the outer ring, and threaded a yellow bead onto each loop so they seemed to hover instead of touching. Where the wire passed close to the nucleus, she glued a strip of felt underneath to insulate the foam from the scratchy ends.

By dinner the atom hung from the light fixture, spinning slowly whenever anyone walked past. Kaylee pointed at each bead in turn, quizzing herself under her breath, red and yellow and white, until Dex leaned over the table and tapped the nucleus.

"Which one's the neutral one?" he asked.

Kaylee tapped the nearest white bead. "That one. No charge at all."

John had come to Grandma's house planning to conquer the harmony part in "Down in the River." He was singing the low line while Grandma sang the high one, and every time they hit the long note at the end of the chorus, he ran out of air and dropped out before she did. Grandma just kept singing, steady as a fence post, and John flopped onto the porch swing and stared at her.

"You breathe sometime," he said. "I've watched you. Nobody holds a note that long."

Grandna smiled and said nothing, which made him more determined than any answer would have.

On Saturday she took him to the church hall, where the River Choir was rehearsing. Thirty singers stood in two curved rows, the sopranos on one side and the altos facing them, and the director raised her hand. "Once more, and this time hold the final note until I cut you off," she said. John sat in the back with a bag of polymer clay beads Grandma was going to bake into earrings later, but he hardly touched it. He watched. The note began, a single unbroken sound, and it went on and on, longer than any breath he had ever taken. He counted. Thirty seconds. Forty-five. The sound never wavered, never thinned.

Then he caught it. The alto in the second row tilted her chin and took a quick breath, and the singer beside her didn't. A second later someone in the back row sneaked a breath of his own. They were taking turns, sneaking air at different moments so the note itself never stopped. It was like watching an intricate rope being braided, each strand going under at a different time, and he had to test it before he'd believe it. He stood up, walked to the empty spot the director pointed to, and on the next long note, he breathed in the middle, quick and sly, right where the singers on either side of him were still holding. The note sailed on without a hole in it.

Afterward he found Grandma by the piano. "It's called staggered breathing, isn't it?" he said. "You take turns."

"Tonight we hold that note together," she said, "and you breathe when the altos breathe."

story:
Tyler sat at his grandmother's kitchen table with his mystery story draft in front of him and a red pen in his hand, because in two days the writing club was meeting again and last time his story had flopped. He knew it had flopped, even though nobody said anything mean. They just sat there, polite and quiet, while he read. "It's a good genre," his friend Marcus had said afterward, "it just sounded, I don't know, bumpy." Tyler wanted this time to be different.

The trouble was, when he read the pages silently, they looked fine to him. Every sentence seemed okay. His grandmother drifted past with a watering can, pausing to sprinkle her African violets on the windowsill. "Still working on the mystery?" she asked. "I nurture those violets for a year before they bloom, you know. Some things take time." Tyler nodded without really hearing. He read the opening again in his head and still couldn't find the bump.

Then he tried something. He read the first paragraph out loud, alone in the kitchen. "The old dark spooky house loomed darkly on the dark hill." His own tongue tripped over it like a shoelace. He tried the next line. "Tom walked up the path. Tom opened the door. Tom went inside." Reading it silently, he'd never noticed how every sentence marched the same length, like boots on pavement. Out loud, he actually stumbled, and stumbling made him hear it.

"Grandma, can I read you something?" he called. She set down the watering can, sat across from him, and listened. He read the whole first page aloud, and every time his voice caught, he marked the spot with the red pen. When he finished, she tapped one sentence. "Right there you slowed down," she said. "The one about the very big enormous shadow. I got lost in the extra words." She had a want of her own, too. "Read me the ending," she said. "I've been dying to know who took the painting." Tyler covered the last page with his hand. "You have to wait like everyone else, Grandma."

He cut the weak adjectives first, the very big enormous shadow becoming just the enormous shadow, the old dark spooky house becoming the crooked house on the hill. Then he broke up the march of same-sized sentences, letting some run long and complex while others stopped abrupt, like a door slamming. Reading aloud, he could hear the difference now, the rhythm shifting when Tom crept through the halls instead of walking, walking, walking.

At the writing club on Thursday, Marcus leaned forward during the part with the hidden painting. When Tyler finished the last line, a short one, the room stayed silent for a second and then everyone started talking at once. "That was so much better," Marcus said. "What'd you change?" Tyler shrugged and clicked his pen. "I made myself trip over it first."

Aurora spread her poster board across the archive table and frowned at it. Her class assignment was a calendar of ancient Egypt, and she had drawn four neat seasons, spring, summer, autumn, winter, because that was what a year had. Her best friend Milo leaned over from the next table, where he was squashing a paper pyramid flat for the third time.

"Mine keeps collapsing," Milo said. "Ancient Egyptians were geniuses. I can't even make one out of cardstock."

Aurora flipped through a folder of copied papyrus records and stopped at a page listing festival months. She counted on her finger. Then she counted again. "Milo. This only has three seasons. Three. Not four." The library lights hummed above them while she traced the strange words with her pencil. One section repeated a word, Akhet, over months that mentioned high water everywhere. Another, Peret, appeared beside drawings of green shoots. The last one, Shemu, matched pictures of sickles and stacked grain. She turned the page slowly, feeling the paper's dry edge, and the pattern almost snapped into place.

"It's the river," she said. "The Nile. Their year follows the water." She grabbed a blank sheet and drew a wide blue curve down the middle. "Look. Akhet, the flood. Then Peret, the growing season. Then Shemu, the harvest." Milo set down his flattened pyramid and stared.

"So they didn't have winter at all? No snow days?" He looked genuinely wounded.

"They had flood days, probably worse." Aurora laughed. She began to incorporate the three seasons into her calendar, splitting the poster into three bright bands with the Nile curving through all of them. She had almost been biased toward four seasons just because that was what she had always known, and that was exactly why the Egyptians hadn't counted that way. Their whole farming year depended on the river, not the sky.

Milo taped a lopsided pyramid onto the corner of her poster. "There. Factor in a pyramid and it's perfect."

Scarlett held the violin under her chin and plucked the A string, and the note wobbled like a fence post about to fall over. That was all. No instructions, no diagram.

The problem was that Scarlett had no idea which way to turn the peg. She remembered last summer at her grandpa's house, when her cousin Marco had tried to tune the old guitar in the den. Marco had cranked a peg with great confidence, and the note had sunk lower and lower, like a whale diving. Grandpa had laughed and said, "Other way, kiddo. Tightening a string raises its pitch. Loosening it lowers it." Marco had turned back the other way and the note climbed up out of the whale depths. Scarlett, watching from the couch, had thought it looked like magic. Now she realized it was more like a rule.

She plucked the string again, then hummed the piano's A in her memory. Her string sat below it, saggy and sour. If her string was too low, then the peg must be too loose. She turned it a tiny bit, plucked, and listened. Still low. Another small turn, and the note rose to meet the one in her head, close enough that the wobble between them slowed like a spinning coin settling.

"Whoa," said Priya from the next stand. Priya wanted first chair more than anything and had been eavesdropping with her whole body. "How did you do that without a tuner?" Scarlett offered the violin over. "String's too low, tighten. Too high, loosen. Want to try your D?" Priya grabbed it, turned the peg the wrong way, and the note dropped so fast they both winced. "Okay," Priya said, wincing. "Whale. I heard the whale."

Scarlett took the violin back and eased the peg forward, and the D climbed up pure and bright, and somewhere down the hall she heard Mr. Herrera's footsteps returning.

She had Grandma's postcard out, the one that said FIND ME, along with the numbers Grandma always scribbled at the bottom: 40, then a little N, then 105, then a little W. story:
Nolan set the recipe card on the counter and read it twice before touching anything, because last time he had tried this, he'd added the salt twice and the muffins had made his little sister Bree gag dramatically at the breakfast table. Today was different. Mom had promised that if he could bake a batch from start to finish, following every step without calling her into the kitchen, the muffins were officially his recipe. Bree wanted one in her lunchbox tomorrow, and she had already picked out which muffin liner she liked best, the one with tiny green frogs on it, so the pressure was real.

He turned the dial to three seventy-five to preheat the oven, mixed the dry ingredients, and then cracked the eggs. One tiny piece of shell went in, and he fished it out with another piece of shell, which somehow worked better than the spoon. When he added the wet ingredients to the dry and stirred, the batter puffed up slightly, like it was breathing. Nolan frowned at it. Batter wasn't supposed to do that, was it? He glanced at the recipe again and noticed a line he'd skimmed past: the batter could rest for a few minutes before going into the oven. That seemed backwards to him. If the batter was already bubbling, letting it sit should make the bubbles disappear, like a forgotten glass of soda.

He remembered a school unit where they'd read that double-acting baking powder releases gas twice, once when it gets wet in the batter and again when it is heated in the oven. He had thought it was boring then, just words on a worksheet, but now he stared at the puffed batter and a whole chain of ideas clicked together. The bubbles he could see were only the first round. The second round had to come from the heat of the oven, so letting the batter wait a few minutes wouldn't ruin anything, because the oven would start a fresh burst of rising. He decided to test it. He filled five muffin cups right away, set the timer for five minutes, and filled the other five cups after the timer buzzed, keeping the two groups on opposite ends of the pan like a tiny experiment.

"Are they done yet?" Bree asked, drifting in barefoot and hovering near the oven, where the smell had started to leak out warm and sweet. "Because I already picked my frog liner, and I'm not sharing it with anyone."

"They need eighteen minutes," Nolan said, watching through the oven door as all the muffins rose, the early ones and the late ones both climbing into rounded golden tops. He couldn't see inside the batter, but he could see the proof, the ones that had waited rose just as proudly as the ones that hadn't. Maybe even a hair taller. He wrote both results on the back of the recipe card, because a good narrator of his own experiment, he decided, should record what actually happened rather than what he expected.

When the muffins came out, Bree claimed the tallest one for her frog liner and pronounced it "actually legendary." Nolan bit into his own and tasted blueberry and lemon and the small, private satisfaction of having figured something out by himself. His grandpa would have been proud; there was a frail old photo of him in his bakery apron on the fridge, and Nolan had started this whole project because he wanted to bake like that someday, not from a box, but for real. He licked a smear of batter off his thumb and slid the recipe card into the drawer next to Grandpa's old wooden spoon.

"Same time next month?" Bree asked, already reaching for a second muffin. "I vote chocolate chip."

Emily slid her French workbook across the library table until it bumped the dictionary, which was the size of a brick and just as heavy. "J'ai une soeur," she read under her breath. "Elle s'appelle Katie." That part felt solid. Across the library, Marcus was building a tower out of encyclopedias, which the librarian pretended not to see. Emily knew Marcus took French too, and Marcus was, in her private opinion, reckless about checking his work. He'd once turned in a whole paragraph about his "horse mother." She carried the napkin over anyway.

"Do you know this word?" she asked. "Avoir?"

"Sure," Marcus said, not looking up. "It's how you say stuff. Watch, I'll do my age." He straightened up and recited, proud and loud enough that the librarian glanced over. "Je suis onze ans. I am eleven."

Isabella slid her notebook across the library table and counted on her fingers for the third time. Seven paragraphs. Mr. Ruiz had said the essay contest entries were due at the end of writing club, forty minutes from now, and her draft was seven paragraphs long.

Aubrey sat on the back step with her poster board and a pencil that had been sharpened down to a stub. The assignment was due Monday: draw a food chain, starting with the sun, ending with a top predator, and be ready to explain what happens if one link disappears. She had the sun. She sketched the clover patch near the fence, then the rabbits that showed up every evening to nibble it. Then she stopped. Something had been visiting the yard at night, something that left a pile of gray fur by the compost bin and knocked over the low-voltage garden lights. She had never seen it. She drew a blank circle at the top of the chain and labeled it with a question mark, because she could not put an animal she had never met into her homework.

While she waited, she turned over an old log to study the pill bugs, tiny decomposers breaking down the dead wood into dark soil, soil that fed the clover. She wrote that on a scrap paper. Then her little brother Marcus stomped out with a granola bar. "What are you doing?" he asked.

"Sorting who eats what," Aubrey said. "The rabbits eat the clover, so they're eating only producers. Animals that eat only producers are called primary consumers." She tapped her pencil. "The thing that eats the rabbits would be a secondary consumer."

"A thing eats rabbits?"

"That's what I'm trying to find out."

The light dimmed. The clover rustled once, then twice. Aubrey held her breath as a red shape stepped out of the shadow of the fence, low and quick, ears pricked toward the rabbit trail. She did not move. She did not even blink. She just slid the poster closer and wrote one word inside the blank circle: fox.

Marcus whispered, "Erase the rabbits and see what happens."

"Then the fox goes hungry," Aubrey whispered back, "and the clover takes over the whole yard."

The fox's amber eyes turned toward the steps.

Lauren put the lamp back and checked on the cricket cabinet, just in case. The latch was open a crack. She shut it fast, then pressed her ear against the door.

Something inside chirped back.

Evelyn pressed the switch three times before the bulb even flickered. The circuit bench at the science museum smelled like pencil shavings and old wire, and her teammate Marcus kept jiggling the battery in its clamp as if that would help. Their project had to work by two o'clock, when the demonstrator came around to see if the bulb could light and, more importantly, if they could explain why. Electricity was invisible, which bothered Evelyn more than anything else at the museum, worse than the fungus display that glowed under glass or the hall of mirrors that refracted the visitors into stretched, wobbling versions of themselves. You could watch a bulb. You could not watch the reason.

"It worked a second ago," Marcus said. He was hesitant about touching the wires again, holding the stripped end above the clip like it might bite. Evelyn traced the loop with her finger, battery to switch to bulb and back, the way the diagram on the wall showed. A circle. Then the bulb went dark for good. Evelyn unscrewed it and shook it near her ear, and something rattled inside, a tiny loose filament. Their one bulb was dead, and the spare bin was empty because the homeschool group from the second floor had cleaned it out an hour ago.

"We're finished," Marcus said.

Evelyn looked at their three spare bulbs, all working, all useless in a single loop. Then she looked at the wall diagram beside the one she knew, the one with two loops. She borrowed two more wires from the bench beside theirs and built a second path, bulb one in the first circle, bulb two in its own circle, both circles touching the battery. When she closed the switch, both glowed.

Marcus unscrewed bulb one. Its light died. The other stayed on, steady and bright, and Marcus actually stood up. "It's still lit! But that one's broken."

"Each bulb has its own path to the battery," Evelyn said, "so the others stay lit if one bulb breaks. It's called a parallel circuit."

The demonstrator stopped at their bench at two o'clock and asked what would happen if she removed a bulb. Evelyn unscrewed one, and the bench still glowed.

Priya, who had insisted the whole trip would be useless, was in the front row, clapping loudest. Afterward she said, "Next time, can I do the committee part?"

"Deal," said Joshua, and he tore a page from his notebook and handed it to her.

John had one job in the spring concert, and it was not going well. He was supposed to sing the low harmony line while Priya carried the melody, and every time they tried, the two lines collapsed into one. Ms. Reyes had left them alone in the studio for ten minutes to practice the Emperor's New March, which was, in Priya's opinion, the most controversial song choice of the decade, since the whole choir had argued about it for a full rehearsal. John leaned over the piano and scrutinized the sheet music, following his line down and her line up with one finger on each. The notes looked different. They sounded the same. That made no sense, and it bothered him like a pebble in his shoe.

Then he noticed something. On the page, his note sat in the bottom space of the staff and hers sat three lines higher, and when he plunked them on the piano, one key then the other, they still felt almost like the same note. "Wait," he said. "Yours is an octave higher than mine." Priya raised an eyebrow. "A what?"

"An octave. That's what it's called when a note is that far apart." He played both keys again. "And I read that a note one octave higher than another vibrates exactly twice as fast, which is why the two sound like the same note at different heights." He hummed his low note, then hers. Same note. Different heights. That was the trick of it: their ears were telling them they matched when they didn't, and their ears were half right.

"Okay," Priya said slowly, "so we're not fighting. We're octaves." They tried the harmony again, and this time John kept his feet planted on his low note like a fence post while her melody floated above it. Ms. Reyes came back in, listened with her eyes closed, and said, "Well, well." Priya grinned and elbowed John. "Told you it was her fault," she whispered, and John sang on.

Grandpa's truck engine knocked on the drive up, a sound like a piston tapping out a complaint, and it stopped only when they reached the campsite beside Miller Lake. Lily climbed out and unfolded the old atlas he kept under the seat. Last summer she had left it out in the rain, and the corners were still rippled and soft. "I need to know where we are," she said. "Exactly." Her parents were hiking the ridge on the far side of the lake, and they had promised to call at noon with their position. Grandpa's phone had no bars. If the call somehow came through on the radio instead, the ranger would want coordinates, not the name of a lake that appeared on half the maps in the county.

The atlas had thin curved lines drawn across it, numbered along the edges. She found a word printed beside the horizontal ones. "They're called parallels," she said slowly, "because they never meet." Her eyes followed two of them across the whole country, side by side, and sure enough, they never crossed. The vertical lines had a name too: meridians. So a place had two numbers, one from each kind of line. She put her finger on the campsite, read sideways to the edge, then up. "Forty-four degrees north, seventy-one west." It felt like holding something solid.

She remembered the rainy afternoon when she'd ruined the atlas, and how she had hidden it under the seat instead of telling him. She could apologize now, or she could keep turning pages and hope he never noticed the water stains. She kept turning pages.

At noon the radio crackled, and her father's voice came through, giving numbers. Lily checked them against the ridge on her map and traced the meridian up from the bottom edge with one finger until it crossed the right parallel. "They're three miles northeast," she told Grandpa, and marked the spot with a pencil stub, pressing hard enough to imply that this crossing, at least, was permanent.

story:
Oliver leaned so close to Maya's basement computer that his nose almost touched the screen. On it, a small orange cat waited inside the Scratch editor, surrounded by stacks of colored blocks like Lego pieces.

"Watch this," Maya said. She dragged a block that said "repeat 10" under a "move 10 steps" block and snapped it in. "Ten copies," Oliver repeated, grinning. "That would take forever." He rubbed his hands together. "Okay. Teach me the whole thing. I want my dodging game done by tonight."

Maya showed him how to draw a falling meteor, then how to make a block that said "if touching the cat, then change score by one." Oliver built it himself, clicking the blocks together until they locked with a satisfying snap. He set the score to count meteors dodged, hit the flag, and steered the cat with his arrow keys.

The first meteor sailed past. The score stayed at zero.

"That's wrong," Oliver said. "I dodged it. It should be one." He slid the cat under the next meteor, letting it whoosh by untouched. Still zero. He frowned at the screen. Nothing looked broken. The blocks were all there, all snapped together, so the problem had to be hiding somewhere he couldn't see, like a knot inside a sneaker.

He had an idea. "The if-then block checks once," he said slowly. "But the meteor is always falling, so it should always be checking." He dragged his if-then block inside a "forever" loop. "Now it integrates the check into the loop, so it runs every single frame." He hit the flag again.

A meteor whisked past the cat. The score jumped to one.

"It works!" Oliver shouted, both fists in the air. "Maya! It works!"

Footsteps thumped down the basement stairs. Maya's grandpa appeared with a plate of crackers, squinting at the screen. "What's all the yelling? You two are just snapping little blocks together?"

"That's the coding," Oliver said proudly. "It's called Scratch. They made it at the MIT Media Lab, and it came out in 2007."

Grandpa set down the plate. "Snapping blocks. In my day we typed everything by hand, line by line, and one typo ruined it all."

"This way it still can break," Oliver said, "but you can see it break." He pointed at his forever loop. "See, this part is durable. Grandpa, watch this one."

He clicked the green flag, and the meteors rained down while the score climbed, two, three, four, and Oliver shouted, "I'm the conductor now!"

story:
Florence stood at the festival's German booth with a tablet in her hands and a poster behind her that said "Beschreibe deine Familie," describe your family. Her task was to write five sentences about her family and pets in German, then read them aloud at the microphone in an hour. She typed her first sentence carefully: "Ich habe einen hund und eine katze." The tablet's spell-checker immediately underlined two words in red, "hund" and "katze," even though she had checked them in the dictionary twice. Why would it flag words she knew were right?

She despised being wrong in public, so she looked for a pattern. She scrolled through the German phrases on the booth's display: "Meine Familie ist groß. Mein Vater hat ein Auto. Wir wohnen in einem Haus." Hund, Katze, Auto, Haus, Vater, Familie. Every single one of those words started with a capital letter, even when it sat in the middle of a sentence. English only did that for names and sentence starters. Was there something about German where every noun began with a capital letter, no matter where it appeared? If that were true, the spell-checker wasn't saying her words were misspelled. It was saying they were lowercased.

Florence decided to test it. She typed "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze," capitalizing both animals, and the red underlines vanished. She tried it again with "Meine Mutter hat zwei Katzen," and nothing was flagged. The pattern held. She laughed at the irony of it: the checker had looked like her enemy when it had actually been teaching her something.

She wrote out all five sentences, watching the screen like it was a transparent window into the language's rules, and every noun got its capital. At the microphone, she read, "Ich habe einen Hund und eine Katze. Meine Schwester hat zwei Kaninchen." The volunteer grinned and said, "Perfekt!"
